notes.definition: Graphene is a single layer of graphite: a sheet of carbon atoms, one atom thick, arranged in hexagonal rings. Fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms with hollow shapes, such as Buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀) and cylindrical carbon nanotubes.
explanation: Graphene is a single layer of graphite. It is a flat sheet of carbon atoms, just one atom thick, in which each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three others to make hexagonal rings. Because it is a single layer, there are no weak forces between layers to slide or break apart, so graphene is extremely strong for its mass: the many strong covalent bonds across the sheet hold it together. As in graphite, one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised, so graphene conducts electricity very well. Being only one atom thick, it is also very light and almost transparent.

These properties make graphene useful in electronics (for example in flexible touchscreens and fast, very thin components) and in composites, where small amounts of graphene are added to other materials to make them stronger and lighter. Remember to explain graphene's properties in terms of structure and bonding: strength from strong covalent bonds, conductivity from delocalised electrons.

Fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms with hollow shapes. Their structure is based on hexagonal rings of carbon atoms, but they may also contain rings with five or seven carbon atoms; these allow the sheet to curve into a closed or tube shape. The first fullerene to be discovered was Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀, which has a spherical shape like a football. It is made of 60 carbon atoms arranged in 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons, with each carbon atom bonded to three others. Unlike diamond and graphite, C₆₀ is a molecule, not a giant structure, so it has weak intermolecular forces between molecules.

Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes. They are like a sheet of graphene rolled into a tube, with a diameter of only about a nanometre but a length that can be many thousands or millions of times greater. They therefore have very high length to diameter ratios. Nanotubes have high tensile strength (they are hard to pull apart) because of their strong covalent bonds, and they conduct electricity because of their delocalised electrons.

The properties of fullerenes make them useful for nanotechnology, electronics and materials. Uses include: delivering drugs into the body (molecules can be carried inside the hollow cages); lubricants (spherical C₆₀ molecules can roll like tiny ball bearings); catalysts (their huge surface area can hold catalyst particles); and reinforcing materials, for example nanotubes added to tennis rackets and bicycle frames to make them strong but light. You need to recognise graphene and fullerenes from diagrams and descriptions, so learn their shapes: a flat single sheet, a hollow sphere, and a hollow tube.
keyFacts: Graphene is a single layer of graphite, one atom thick.
In graphene each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds, making hexagonal rings.
Graphene is very strong (strong covalent bonds) and conducts electricity (delocalised electrons).
Graphene is useful in electronics and composites.
Fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms with hollow shapes.
Fullerenes are based on hexagonal rings but may also contain rings of five or seven carbon atoms.
Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀, was the first fullerene discovered; it is spherical.
Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes with very high length to diameter ratios.
Uses of fullerenes include drug delivery, lubricants, catalysts and reinforcing materials such as tennis rackets.

keyTerms.definition: A single layer of graphite: a sheet of carbon atoms one atom thick, in hexagonal rings.
A molecule of carbon atoms with a hollow shape, based on hexagonal rings and sometimes rings of five or seven atoms.
C₆₀, the first fullerene discovered: a hollow spherical molecule of 60 carbon atoms.
A cylindrical fullerene, like a rolled-up sheet of graphene, with a very high length to diameter ratio.
Length divided by diameter. For nanotubes it is very large because they are extremely long and narrow.
A material made of two or more materials combined, such as a plastic reinforced with graphene or nanotubes.

equations.name: Length to diameter ratio
equations.formula: length to diameter ratio = length ÷ diameter
equations.symbols: ratio = L ÷ d (same units for both)

workedExamples.title: Length to diameter ratio of a nanotube
workedExamples.question: A carbon nanotube is 0.2 mm long and has a diameter of 1 nm. Calculate its length to diameter ratio. (1 mm = 10⁻³ m, 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m)
steps: Convert both to metres: length = 0.2 × 10⁻³ m = 2 × 10⁻⁴ m; diameter = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m.
workedExamples.answer: 2 × 10⁵ (200 000): the nanotube is 200 000 times longer than it is wide.

workedExamples.title: Relative formula mass of C₆₀
workedExamples.question: Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀. (Ar of C = 12)

workedExamples.title: Counting bonds in C₆₀
workedExamples.question: In C₆₀ each carbon atom is bonded to three other carbon atoms. How many carbon to carbon bonds are in one molecule?
steps: Each bond joins two atoms, so it has been counted twice.

diagrams.title: Graphene
diagrams.caption: Graphene is a single layer of graphite, one atom thick. Each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds in hexagonal rings, and one electron per atom is delocalised.

diagrams.title: Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀
diagrams.caption: A hollow spherical molecule of 60 carbon atoms. Each corner is a carbon atom bonded to three others. The structure contains 20 hexagonal rings (one shaded blue) and 12 pentagonal rings (one shaded red). Faint lines are bonds on the far side.

diagrams.title: A carbon nanotube
diagrams.caption: A cylindrical fullerene, like a sheet of graphene rolled into a tube. Its diameter is about a nanometre but it can be very long, so it has a very high length to diameter ratio.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think graphene is weak because it is so thin.
misconceptions.right: In fact graphene is extremely strong for its mass because every atom is held by strong covalent bonds across the sheet.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think fullerenes contain only hexagonal rings.
misconceptions.right: In fact fullerenes are based on hexagonal rings but may also contain rings of five or seven carbon atoms. C₆₀ has 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think C₆₀ is a giant covalent structure like diamond.
misconceptions.right: In fact C₆₀ is a molecule of 60 atoms. Its molecules are held to each other by weak intermolecular forces.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often confuse graphene with graphite.
misconceptions.right: In fact graphene is one single layer; graphite is many layers stacked with weak forces between them.

realWorld: Carbon nanotubes are added to tennis rackets, bicycle frames and golf clubs to make them strong but light.
Graphene is being developed for flexible touchscreens, faster electronic components and stronger, lighter composite materials.
Fullerene cages are being researched for delivering drugs to specific places in the body.
examTips: Learn the definitions word for word: 'graphene is a single layer of graphite' and 'fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms with hollow shapes'.
When explaining graphene's strength, say 'strong covalent bonds'; for its conductivity, say 'delocalised electrons'.
Be ready to give uses of fullerenes: drug delivery, lubricants, catalysts, reinforcing materials (nanotubes in tennis rackets), electronics.
In length to diameter calculations, convert both measurements to the same unit before dividing; the answer has no units.
summary: Graphene is a single layer of graphite, one atom thick.
Graphene is strong (covalent bonds) and conducts (delocalised electrons): useful in electronics and composites.
Fullerenes are hollow carbon molecules based on hexagonal rings, sometimes with five- or seven-membered rings.
C₆₀ (Buckminsterfullerene) is spherical and was the first fullerene discovered.
Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes with very high length to diameter ratios.
Fullerenes are used in nanotechnology, electronics, materials, drug delivery, lubricants and catalysts.

options: A single layer of graphite
A form of diamond
A hollow sphere of carbon atoms
A polymer of carbon and hydrogen
markScheme: 1 mark: A single layer of graphite
questions.explanation: Graphene is one layer of graphite, one atom thick. A hollow sphere describes C₆₀.

questions.question: What is the formula of Buckminsterfullerene?
options: C₆
C₂₀
C₆₀
C₁₀₀
markScheme: 1 mark: C₆₀
questions.explanation: Buckminsterfullerene is C₆₀, a spherical molecule of 60 carbon atoms.

questions.question: What shape is a carbon nanotube?
options: Sphere
Flat sheet
Cube
Cylinder
markScheme: 1 mark: Cylinder
questions.explanation: Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes. A sphere is C₆₀ and a flat sheet is graphene.

questions.question: Which statement describes fullerenes?
options: Giant ionic lattices of carbon
Molecules of carbon atoms with hollow shapes
Layers of carbon atoms held by weak forces
Carbon atoms each bonded to four others in a 3D network
markScheme: 1 mark: Molecules of carbon atoms with hollow shapes
questions.explanation: Fullerenes are hollow carbon molecules. Layers describe graphite, and four bonds in 3D describes diamond.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows part of a sheet of graphene.
Why does graphene conduct electricity?
options: It contains ions that can move
Each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds
It has delocalised electrons that can move across the sheet
Its layers slide over each other
markScheme: 1 mark: It has delocalised electrons that can move across the sheet
questions.explanation: One electron per carbon atom is delocalised, as in graphite. Graphene has no ions and is only one layer, so sliding layers are not involved.

questions.question: Which rings can be found in the structure of fullerenes?
options: Only rings of six carbon atoms
Rings of six carbon atoms, and sometimes rings of five or seven
Only rings of five carbon atoms
Rings of four and eight carbon atoms
markScheme: 1 mark: Rings of six carbon atoms, and sometimes rings of five or seven
questions.explanation: Fullerenes are based on hexagonal rings, but may also contain rings of five or seven carbon atoms, which let the structure curve.

questions.question: Why are carbon nanotubes used to reinforce tennis rackets?
options: They are very strong for their low mass
They conduct electricity
They are hollow so they absorb water
They have low melting points so they are easy to shape
markScheme: 1 mark: They are very strong for their low mass
questions.explanation: Nanotubes have very high tensile strength and are very light, so a small amount strengthens a material without adding much mass.

questions.question: Which property of fullerenes allows them to be used to deliver drugs into the body?
options: They conduct electricity
They have hollow shapes that can carry other molecules
They are very hard
They are made of layers that slide
markScheme: 1 mark: They have hollow shapes that can carry other molecules
questions.explanation: The hollow cages of fullerenes can carry drug molecules inside them.

options: A giant covalent structure like diamond
A fullerene molecule
A single layer of graphite
A polymer
markScheme: 1 mark: A fullerene molecule
questions.explanation: A hollow ball of 60 carbon atoms is C₆₀, a fullerene molecule. It is not giant (it has a fixed number of atoms) and it is not a flat layer.

questions.question: Why does C₆₀ have a much lower melting point than graphite?
options: C₆₀ has weaker covalent bonds
C₆₀ is made of molecules with weak intermolecular forces between them, whereas melting graphite breaks strong covalent bonds
C₆₀ contains more delocalised electrons
C₆₀ has ionic bonds
markScheme: 1 mark: C₆₀ is made of molecules with weak intermolecular forces between them, whereas melting graphite breaks strong covalent bonds
questions.explanation: C₆₀ is a molecular substance: only weak intermolecular forces are overcome when it melts. Graphite is giant covalent, so covalent bonds must be broken.

questions.question: How thick is a sheet of graphene?
options: One atom thick
Ten atoms thick
About 1 mm thick
The same thickness as a pencil lead
markScheme: 1 mark: One atom thick
questions.explanation: Graphene is a single layer of graphite, so it is just one atom thick.

questions.question: Which statement about carbon nanotubes is correct?
options: They have a very low length to diameter ratio
They are made of ions
They have a very high length to diameter ratio
They contain only rings of five carbon atoms
markScheme: 1 mark: They have a very high length to diameter ratio
questions.explanation: Nanotubes are very long and very narrow, so their length to diameter ratio is very high.

questions.question:
Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of C₆₀.
Relative atomic mass (Ar): C = 12
questions.explanation: Multiply the number of carbon atoms by the relative atomic mass: 60 × 12 = 720.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the dimensions of a carbon nanotube.
Calculate the length to diameter ratio of the nanotube.
1 μm = 1000 nm
markScheme: 1 mark: 1.5 μm = 1500 nm
questions.explanation: Put both in the same unit first. 1.5 μm = 1500 nm, so the ratio is 1500 ÷ 1.5 = 1000. Dividing 1.5 by 1.5 without converting gives the wrong answer of 1.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the dimensions of a carbon nanotube.
Calculate the length to diameter ratio of the nanotube.
1 mm = 1 × 10⁻³ m
1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.5 mm = 5 × 10⁻⁴ m and 1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m
questions.explanation: In metres, the length is 5 × 10⁻⁴ m. Dividing by 1 × 10⁻⁹ m gives 5 × 10⁵ (500 000).

questions.question:
In a C₆₀ molecule each carbon atom is bonded to three other carbon atoms.
Calculate the number of carbon to carbon bonds in one C₆₀ molecule.
questions.explanation: Multiplying atoms by bonds per atom counts every bond twice (once from each end), so divide by 2: 60 × 3 ÷ 2 = 90.

questions.question:
Graphite is made of stacked layers of graphene.
Table 1 shows information about a flake of graphite.
Estimate the number of layers of graphene in the flake.
1 mm = 10⁶ nm
questions.explanation: Convert to nanometres: 0.67 × 10⁶ = 670 000 nm. Then divide by the layer spacing: 670 000 ÷ 0.335 = 2.0 × 10⁶ layers.

questions.question: State what is meant by graphene.
acceptedAnswers: one atom thick layer of carbon
markScheme: 1 mark: a single layer of graphite
questions.explanation: The AQA definition is 'a single layer of graphite'.

questions.question: Name the first fullerene to be discovered.
markScheme: 1 mark: Buckminsterfullerene / C₆₀
questions.explanation: Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀, was discovered first. It is spherical.

questions.question: Give two uses of fullerenes.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: drug delivery into the body; lubricants; catalysts; reinforcing materials (for example tennis rackets); electronics; nanotechnology
questions.explanation: Each use links to a property: hollow cages (drug delivery), spherical molecules (lubricants), large surface area (catalysts), strength (reinforcement).

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows part of a sheet of graphene.
Explain why graphene is very strong.
acceptedAnswers: each carbon bonded to three others
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon atoms joined by strong covalent bonds (each to three others)
1 mark: (in a continuous sheet so) many bonds must be broken to break it
questions.explanation: Strength comes from the network of strong covalent bonds across the sheet.

questions.question: Explain why graphene is useful in electronics.
markScheme: 1 mark: it conducts electricity / is very thin, light and strong
1 mark: because it has delocalised electrons (one per carbon atom) that can move and carry charge
questions.explanation: Electronic components need to conduct, and graphene's delocalised electrons allow this in a sheet just one atom thick.

1 mark: with weak intermolecular forces, so they can roll / slide over each other (like tiny ball bearings)
questions.explanation: The round shape and weak forces between molecules let them move past each other easily, reducing friction.

questions.question: Suggest why fullerenes, including nanotubes, are useful as catalysts or catalyst supports.
acceptedAnswers: high surface area to volume ratio
markScheme: 1 mark: they have a very large surface area (for their mass)
1 mark: so catalyst particles can be attached / reactants have more surface to react on

markScheme: Indicative content: graphene: single layer of graphite; one atom thick; each carbon bonded to three others by covalent bonds; hexagonal rings; flat sheet; delocalised electrons. Use: electronics or composites. C₆₀: fullerene; molecule of 60 carbon atoms; hollow spherical shape; hexagonal and pentagonal rings (20 hexagons, 12 pentagons); each carbon bonded to three others. Use: drug delivery, lubricant or catalyst.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear and correct descriptions of both structures with an appropriate use for each.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): a partial description of one or both structures, or uses given with little structural detail.
questions.explanation: Strong answers give the key structural features of each (flat single layer versus hollow sphere) and a correct use for each.

questions.question:
Graphene and carbon nanotubes are being used to make new materials for electronics and sports equipment.
Explain how the structure and bonding of graphene and carbon nanotubes give them properties that make them suitable for these uses.
markScheme: Indicative content: graphene is a single layer of graphite, one atom thick; nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes, like rolled sheets of graphene; both have carbon atoms each bonded to three others by strong covalent bonds; in hexagonal rings; many strong covalent bonds, so very strong (high tensile strength); very thin / low mass so strong for their mass; ideal for reinforcing composites in sports equipment such as tennis rackets and bike frames; one electron per carbon atom is delocalised; delocalised electrons move and carry charge; so they conduct electricity; useful in electronics; nanotubes have very high length to diameter ratio, useful as tiny conducting wires in nanotechnology.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed and coherent explanation linking strong covalent bonds to strength and delocalised electrons to conductivity, applied to both uses and both materials.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains either strength or conductivity clearly in terms of structure, with some link to uses.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements of properties or uses with little reference to structure and bonding.
questions.explanation: The two key links are strong covalent bonds (strength, so composites and sports equipment) and delocalised electrons (conductivity, so electronics).

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a type of fullerene.
It is a cylinder with a very high length to diameter ratio.
Name this type of fullerene.
markScheme: 1 mark: (carbon) nanotubes
questions.explanation: Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes; their length can be many thousands of times their diameter.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the structures of two forms of carbon, A and B.
A is a flat sheet of carbon atoms, one atom thick, arranged in hexagons.
B is a hollow tube made of the same pattern of hexagons.
Identify A and B.
markScheme: 1 mark: first diagram: graphene
1 mark: second diagram: carbon nanotube
questions.explanation: A flat, single-atom-thick sheet is graphene; the same sheet rolled into a cylinder is a carbon nanotube.
